strengths: The proposed combination of probability-integral-transform scores, a logit transform, and Wasserstein matching is intuitive and readily compatible with differentiable inverse-problem solvers.

The experiments provide promising evidence of sustained reconstruction quality during prolonged optimization. DIP results include improvements over oracle peak MSE performance at higher noise levels, and PET experiments demonstrate benefits when combined with regularization.
The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, noise-level and resolution sweeps, additional images, a deconvolution example, and computational benchmarks.
The paper explicitly acknowledges that distributional calibration does not identify the correct signal and that architectural or explicit priors remain necessary.
weaknesses: The theoretical support contains substantive errors. Corollary B.3 omits the finite-observation sampling term: with zero signal error and fixed N, letting M grow makes its stated bound approach zero although the empirical residual distribution still differs from the population logistic distribution. Proposition B.2 also needs explicit tail or integrability assumptions; Lipschitz continuity of the CDF alone does not control the unbounded derivative of logit. The assertion that tail contributions are negligible does not establish the claimed bound.

The central claims about preventing noise overfitting exceed what aggregate calibration establishes. Sorting discards spatial correspondence and does not test residual independence or conditional calibration. Data-dependent estimates can therefore retain or introduce structured errors while matching the target distribution. The acknowledged sign-flipped-noise example illustrates this limitation, but the paper provides neither sufficient conditions nor systematic experiments establishing when optimization selects accurate solutions. Its finite-sample claim that this example attains exactly the same DC loss as the truth is also generally false.

The evaluation remains too limited for the breadth of the claims: a handful of natural images, one simulated 2D BrainWeb phantom, and a synthetic sinusoidal signal. Five-seed uncertainty is reported for selected DIP experiments, but there is no dataset-level aggregate evaluation or comparable uncertainty analysis for the central PET gains. Robustness to noise-model misspecification and realistic PET acquisition effects is not established.

Important comparisons and controls are missing. These include practical DIP early-stopping methods, discrepancy-principle or residual-statistics stopping rules, and a simple residual-variance matching objective to isolate the benefit of full distribution matching. For clipped Gaussian denoising, DC explicitly models clipping while MSE is not the corresponding likelihood; comparison against a correctly specified censored likelihood and unclipped Gaussian experiments would separate calibration gains from noise-model advantages.

The Poisson experiments deliberately use a non-randomized PIT, whose population target is not uniform. Figure F1 documents a systematic mismatch that increases at lower counts, making the low-dose reconstruction claim particularly sensitive to this approximation. Mentioning randomized PIT without evaluating it leaves unresolved whether the chosen objective biases reconstructed activity. Algorithm 4 also disagrees with Equation 72: its upper-tail approximation uses -m log(q) instead of -(m+1) log(q), changing the gradient.

The regularization interpretation is insufficiently supported. Smaller optimal beta values are not meaningful evidence by themselves because NLL and DC have different scales, and the displayed definitions use a summed NLL versus an averaged DC loss. Moreover, Appendix F.4 uses an image-dependent, nonconvex edge penalty rather than standard TV. Comparisons with normalized objectives, conventional TV, matched non-negativity constraints, and controlled optimization are needed before attributing the improvement to reduced conflict between fidelity and regularization.

Novelty is inadequately positioned against minimum-distance estimation, residual-distribution matching, and classical discrepancy principles. Reproducibility and practicality also remain incomplete: code is only promised for the discussion period, while Appendix G reports approximately 0.5-second DC forward evaluations at one million measurements versus millisecond or submillisecond pointwise losses. End-to-end time-to-quality comparisons are needed to substantiate the practical plug-in claim.

strengths: The proposed combination of probability-integral-transform residuals, a logit transform, and Wasserstein matching is intuitive and offers a potentially useful alternative data-fidelity objective.

The experiments provide encouraging evidence of stable late-iteration reconstruction. DIP results include comparisons against peak MSE-based PSNR, multiple noise levels, and five random seeds; PET experiments also examine explicit regularization and varying image resolution.

The appendices provide substantial derivations, implementation pseudocode, additional examples, and runtime measurements. The discussion appropriately acknowledges that distributional calibration alone does not identify the true signal.
weaknesses: The strongest claims exceed what distributional matching establishes. A calibrated residual histogram does not ensure spatial independence or accurate reconstruction, and data-dependent estimates can retain or introduce noise while achieving low DC loss. Section 4.2 itself demonstrates this ambiguity. Its sign-flipped residual example is not a proven finite-sample worst-case bound, nor does it attain exactly the same empirical loss for arbitrary reference samples. The claimed prevention of overfitting should be restricted to the observed experiments.

The theoretical error analysis contains substantive gaps. Corollary B.3, Equation 47, omits the finite-N empirical residual error: with zero signal error and fixed N, its right-hand side vanishes as M increases, although the empirical residual distribution remains a positive Wasserstein distance from the population distribution. Proposition B.2 also requires control near CDF endpoints; CDF Lipschitz continuity alone does not provide the uniform or integrable logit sensitivity needed for the stated expectation bound. The assertion that tails contribute negligibly does not establish this.

The Poisson application uses an incorrectly calibrated population target at low counts. The ordinary discrete PIT is not uniform, and Figure F1 visibly confirms a discrepancy even for the true phantom. Randomized PIT is discussed but not evaluated. This is particularly relevant to the lower-dose regularized experiment. Moreover, Algorithm 4's upper-tail expression uses -m log(q), whereas Equation 72 correctly uses -(m+1) log(q), leaving uncertainty about the implemented loss and gradients.

Evaluation remains too narrow for the broad practical claims. Quantitative denoising evidence centers on one image, with several additional illustrative images; PET uses one simulated 2D BrainWeb phantom without demonstrated generalization across subjects or real acquisitions. There are no comparisons with practical DIP early-stopping methods, discrepancy-principle approaches, or residual-whiteness objectives. MLEM already achieves a better minimum error in the main unregularized PET experiment, so the demonstrated advantage there is stability rather than best reconstruction accuracy.

The regularization interpretation is confounded by objective scaling. Equation 8 defines NLL as a sum, whereas DC is averaged over measurements. Consequently, orders-of-magnitude differences in optimal beta do not establish reduced conflict between fidelity and regularization. The nonstandard, intensity-dependent edge-preserving penalty also warrants comparison with conventional TV. Better reconstruction at each method's optimal beta is useful evidence, but the causal explanation requires normalized objectives and additional regularizers.

Novelty is insufficiently positioned against minimum-distance estimation, goodness-of-fit objectives, statistical discrepancy principles, and residual-distribution constraints. The related-work discussion is brief, and there are no ablations isolating the benefit of full distribution matching over a noise-energy constraint, the logit transform, or stochastic reference sampling versus deterministic quantiles.

Practical efficiency and reproducibility remain unresolved. Appendix G reports roughly 0.5 seconds for a million-element DC forward pass versus approximately 0.0008–0.0022 seconds for MSE/NLL, but does not establish matched-quality end-to-end efficiency. Source code is promised for a later discussion period rather than supplied in the manuscript, which makes the consequential pseudocode discrepancy and numerical boundary handling harder to verify.

strengths: The proposed PIT–logit–Wasserstein loss is conceptually simple and addresses a meaningful problem: reducing noise fitting during prolonged optimization of inverse problems.

The experiments provide promising evidence of stable late-iteration performance. DIP results include multiple noise levels, five random seeds, and additional images; PET and synthetic deconvolution broaden the demonstration.

The manuscript provides extensive implementation details, numerical approximations, pseudocode, and runtime measurements. It also explicitly acknowledges that distributional consistency does not uniquely identify the true signal.
weaknesses: The central interpretation exceeds what the objective establishes. Matching the aggregate residual distribution does not establish residual independence, spatial whiteness, or accurate reconstruction. Permuting residuals preserves the loss while potentially changing reconstruction quality substantially. Appendix B acknowledges this ambiguity, but repeated claims that DC prevents overfitting or removes the conflict with regularization remain insufficiently qualified.

The theoretical analysis contains substantive gaps. Corollary B.3, Equation 47, omits the finite-N empirical sampling error: with zero signal error and fixed N, the expected distance to the logistic population remains positive as M grows. Proposition B.2 also needs explicit control of the unbounded logit derivative; the footnote asserting that tails contribute negligibly does not supply that control.

The PET implementation does not satisfy its exact calibration premise: it uses non-randomized Poisson CDF values, whose distribution is not uniform even at the truth. Figure F1 shows this mismatch, especially at lower counts, yet the randomized PIT alternative is not evaluated. Its effect on reconstruction bias and the low-dose results therefore remains unresolved.

The evaluation is insufficiently competitive or comprehensive. DIP comparisons primarily use vanilla MSE training, without practical early-stopping methods or discrepancy-based alternatives. PET uses one simulated 2D phantom, without convincing reconstruction-level uncertainty estimates or broader data validation; MLEM already achieves better peak error in the unregularized example. Noise-model misspecification and the choices of logit transform, Wasserstein distance, and stochastic reference sampling are not adequately ablated.

Some comparisons have important confounds. DIP uses clipped Gaussian observations, for which ordinary MSE is not the matched likelihood; improvements at high noise may partly reflect better treatment of clipping. The claim that much smaller regularization weights demonstrate less conflict is also unsupported without matching objective scales: Equation 5 averages DC over measurements, whereas Equation 8 sums NLL. PET methods additionally differ in non-negativity enforcement and masking.

Novelty is inadequately positioned against minimum-distance estimation, residual-distribution matching, and classical discrepancy principles. The available evidence establishes a promising heuristic, but not yet a sufficiently differentiated and validated contribution for acceptance. Reproducibility is also incomplete because code is only promised for the discussion period.
